questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis by First Rewriting the Function
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094530/assets/9e19c1cd8bca76f1eec39acfa1b09c0f08b67faea5ddce8325e093923d21d394.png)

Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1},$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+1} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{3}{4}|=\frac{3}{4}.$

questions.problem: Find the area between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{\frac{x+1}{4}},$ the $y$-axis, and the lines $y=-1$ and $y=0.$
questions.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{\frac{x+1}{4}} \\ {y}^{3} & =\frac{x+1}{4} \\ 4{y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & =4{y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(4{y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =4{\int }_{-1}^{0}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{-1}^{0}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={y}^{4}{|}_{-1}^{0}-y{|}_{-1}^{0} \\  & =(0-1)-(0+1) \\  & =-2\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-2|=2.$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Finite Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis
questions.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094530/assets/fb622d0d4c25753001c6f51192a587f3fefed20474333c4564c37f65e5969a89.png)

Find the area of the finite region bounded between the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis, as shown above.
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡y & =0 \\ y & =0,\pm \pi ,…\end{aligned}
$$

From the diagram, we see that we want to find the area between the curve $x=\operatorname{sin}⁡y$ and the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=\pi .$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡y\,\text{d}y \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡y{|}_{0}^{\pi } \\  & =-\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi )+\operatorname{cos}⁡(0) \\  & =-(-1)+1 \\  & =2\end{aligned}
$$

questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}3y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{2}y(6-y) & =0 \\ y & =0,6\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094530/assets/4d5f6214785ff51d2254d8e9a2f7b15e811df643c3a664ee46b56744ede46e53.png)

We want the area between the curve $x=3y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}$ and the $y$-axis from $y=0$ to $y=6.$
To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y & ={\int }_{0}^{6}(3y-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & =3{\int }_{0}^{6}y\,\text{d}y-\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{0}^{6}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}\,{|}_{0}^{6}-\frac{1}{6}{y}^{3}\,{|}_{0}^{6} \\  & =\frac{3}{2}(36-0)-\frac{1}{6}(216-0) \\  & =54-36 \\  & =18\end{aligned}
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Finding the Finite Area Bounded Between a Curve and the Y-Axis
questions.worked_solution:
First, we find the $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{9}{y}^{5}-\frac{1}{9}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3} & =0 \\ \frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}({y}^{2}-y-6) & =0 \\ \frac{1}{9}{y}^{3}(y+2)(y-3) & =0 \\ y & =-2,\,0,\,3\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14094530/assets/8bc9294352d263d7ff57eb257dae9a584b47927b18268ed0ddbe13ba0e2141ce.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=\frac{1}{9}{y}^{5}-\frac{1}{9}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}$ and the $y$-axis from  $y=0$ to $y=3.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}(\frac{1}{9}{y}^{5}-\frac{1}{9}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3})\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{5}\,\text{d}y-\frac{1}{9}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y-\frac{2}{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{9}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{6}}{6}\,|}_{0}^{3}-\frac{1}{9}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}\,|}_{0}^{3}-\frac{2}{3}\cdot {\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}\,|}_{0}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{9}(\frac{243}{2}-0)-\frac{1}{9}(\frac{243}{5}-0)-\frac{2}{3}(\frac{81}{4}-0) \\  & =\frac{27}{2}-\frac{27}{5}-\frac{27}{2} \\  & =-\frac{27}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So, the area that we want is

$$
A=|-\frac{27}{5}|=\frac{27}{5}.
$$
